speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, therefore, propose to share the 20 minutes of speaking time allotted to me, with them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On 4 November 2020, I asked the hon Minister for Law and Home Affairs in this House about the merits of having a separate Judicial Service Commission (JSC) principally to deepen the competence of judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I am not alone in asking for the set-up of the JSC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hon Members of Parliament from both sides of the House have made similar calls for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Minister's reply to my question was that in the current circumstances, the integrated Legal Service Commission (LSC) model that we have for the Legal Service is probably best for the time being.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I agree with the hon Minister that the integrated model served Singapore well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The LSC contributed indelibly to the upholding of the rule of law in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It ensured that our Judiciary is both independent and impartial.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Our Judiciary is held in great esteem not just within Singapore but also internationally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The upholding of the rule of law in Singapore has directly resulted in Singapore's growth as an inclusive nation with good outcomes in education, opportunities for all, irrespective of race, religion or gender, care for the less fortunate, cohesion amongst people and low crime rates.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: What is good for today, however, may not be adequate for tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is our work to improve our institutions over the years that has made us what we are.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The point we should consider today is whether the integrated LSC model, which has served us well, needs to be adjusted with regard to the evolving responsibilities that will be placed on the Judiciary in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The main arguments I make in support of this Motion are as follows.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Considering the increasing factual and legal complexities of the cases presented in Court, quickening the pace of specialisation amongst our Judges will better equip them with the skills, tools, especially technological tools, and experience to discharge their solemn duties consistently and at the highest standards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Additionally, with the autonomous power to recruit, the JSC can exercise more flexibility and use a wider range of talents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For example, someone with experience in programming can be trained and taught law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Then, he or she can navigate the technical facts of a case much better than a legally trained Judge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That is a deeper, more specialised approach to intentionally growing our judicial service.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Nonetheless, I must acknowledge that I make these points drawing from merely my own knowledge and experience as a legislator and a private legal practitioner.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hence, I am calling on the Government to study the feasibility of my proposal rather than presenting a specific case for it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Specialisation amongst Judges should not mean higher costs for litigants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Rather, what I have in mind is the opposite.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With greater specialisation, our Judges will be more efficient and productive and in a position to further rein in legal costs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The end state that I envision is a specialist Judiciary that ensures that its decisions remain consistently of the highest quality and delivered with due despatch.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Furthermore, it should allow litigants using its processes to be satisfied that they have been provided with good access to justice, their cases have been heard and they have been treated fairly and impartially.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Lastly, it is responsive and keeps abreast of fast-paced developments, particularly technological developments, that are making cases more complex.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One good example of a technological development arose last year when the Court of Appeal had to deal with novel legal issues arising in the world of cryptocurrency algorithmic trading.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: A specialist Judiciary that can achieve all these will strengthen our public's trust, confidence and respect in our legal system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I now make the case for further specialisation of the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I say "further specialisation" because the Judiciary has already developed specialist routes for some years now in response to the increasing complexity of cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Family Justice Courts were set up out of the recognition that family justice is a specialist discipline that requires specific focus and jurisprudential development.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There have been dedicated specialist commercial lists in the General Division of the High Court in areas, such as building and construction, finance, securities, insolvency and trusts, and arbitration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As a private practitioner in active legal practice for some time now, it is clear to me that the Judiciary continues to hear and decide on more complex cases over the years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is not easy to measure complexity of the cases in our Courts objectively but there are several proxies that can provide rough and ready guides.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In an article titled "The Development of Singapore Law: A Bicentennial Retrospective" by the hon Andrew Phang JA, Prof Goh Yihan SC and Prof Jerrold Soh, it is stated that the average reported judgment comprised 4,763 words in 2002.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Now, the average count hovers around 11,000 words.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This statistic is for judgments of both the State Court and the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There is also an upward trend of Singapore cases being cited and commented on overseas, including in the UK and Australian courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is an indication that our Courts are increasingly having to grapple with frontier legal issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: First, the UK Supreme Court had occasion to cite two decisions of the Singapore Court of Appeal in its 2015 judgment on requirements to imply a term in contract law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Next, the New South Wales Supreme Court in 2016 quoted observations of the Singapore High Court on the role of liquidators in legal proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, our Judges carry out a key element of providing order in society, not just in Singapore but, at times, in other Common Law countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Our Legal Service has grown significantly, too, over the years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In 1965, our year of Independence, we had 45 officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In 2014, in recognition of the need to specialise, our Prime Minister announced the restructuring of the Legal Service which involved the introduction of two separate career tracks, judicial and legal, for Legal Service Officers, LSOs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, the specialisation tracks are geared towards the middle ranks of the Legal Service.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Junior and senior officers still operate under a fully integrated model, in respect of their career tracks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Respectfully, given the requirements of the future that I have alluded to, I would think it is good to reconsider the central management of junior and senior officers deployed for judicial duties by the LSC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It seems to me there is a need to plan for longer runways for the junior officers within specific career tracks leading to deeper specialisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Even at the top, the senior LSOs in the Judiciary must devote time and effort to continually upskill themselves so as to keep up with the requirements of their jobs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The establishment of a JSC, with its own secretariat, can help.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At this point in our country's development, there is also sufficient ballast in terms of the number of LSOs currently serving and expected to serve as judicial officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would not pretend that I have dealt with all the issues in my short speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The LSC has evolved over the years to adapt to the changing operating environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Motion calls on the Government to rethink our talent management frameworks and development of LSOs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a practitioner, I have myself seen how much the legal profession as a whole has changed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are part of the Public Service and also form a substantial proportion of the legal profession in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is, therefore, important that they keep pace with the changes that are disrupting the profession.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, digital trends and technology have expanded the frontiers of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One example of a trend needing to be checked is the proliferation of online services on the dark web which have facilitated the rise of complex cross-border cyber crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This calls for deeper expertise, amongst not just our law enforcement agencies, but also our prosecutors.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another example is the increasing use of artificial intelligence in various fields from financial services to legal services and even healthcare.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has given rise to many novel questions of law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One need only to look at the increase in the number of law reform reports that have been published in various jurisdictions in this area.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our very own Singapore Academy of Law has published three reports in the past year in this area alone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I admit that there is a delicate balance to be drawn between specialisation and breadth of experience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As some have said, the world today needs not generalists per se, but deep generalists.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are lateral thinkers who can effectively combine different strands of thought and lessons from different contexts to produce innovative results.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What we need is for both legal and judicial officers to pick up depth and breadth in a select number of specific disciplines or specialised areas in a way that allows them to synthesise skills and knowledge and, in so doing, helps the Government innovate in a fast-changing world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the growth in the size of the Legal Service and the growth in the complexity of the work in both the legal and the judicial branches, there are now adequate sub-specialisations within each branch that facilitate the development of such deep generalists.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because I am of the firm belief that breadth of exposure is key to the proper development and training of a Legal Service Officer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This belief is born out of my own personal experiences as an LSO in the early days of my career.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I started my career as a Judicial Officer, then was posted to the AGC and then was posted back to the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I declare my interest in speaking on the Motion as a practising lawyer as I do appear before Judges in the course of my work.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The Judiciary is one of the three branches of Government; the other two being the Legislature and the Executive.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As an independent public institution, the role of the Judiciary is to uphold the law and ensure justice is accessible to all the citizens of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As our former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong observed, there is a high level of trust in the quality and incorruptibility of our judicial system and infrastructure, a strength that has anchored Singapore's economic development.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our present Chief Justice also recently said: society's regard for and trust in the Courts are extremely precious.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: When I first started legal practice 32 years ago, we only had the Supreme Court and the Subordinate Courts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Over the years, the laws have developed to cater to our changing society and changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The global economy has also changed and our judicial system needs to keep up with such changes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Today, we have increased specialisation to cater to a more diverse population, changing needs and more complex cases.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, the Criminal Courts need to deal with brilliant and sophisticated criminal minds trying to cheat innocent victims of their monies; the Civil Courts have to deal with some of the very complicating civil disputes; intellectual property litigation often involves cross-border disputes and disputes involving sophisticated financial instruments.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: We also have the Family Justice Courts (FJC); the Community Dispute Resolution Tribunal (CDRT); the Employment Claims Tribunal; and, lastly, the Protection from Harassment Court, all of which require specialised skills in the dispensation of justice to different categories of litigants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Judicial officers play an important role in the administration of justice, all the more so for State Court Judicial Officers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: These officers need more specialised skills and more specialised knowledge to better understand the complex facts and how to apply the law to these facts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They need to have good judicial temperament and show empathy in dealing with members of the public and firmness in dealing with criminals.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As a family law practitioner, I wish to share that Judges need to deal sensitively with spouses who are highly emotional and they need to deal sensitively with children as well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The LSC has played a very important role in staffing the Judiciary, the AGC and the various agencies like the Insolvency Office, Public Trustee's Office, Legal Aid Bureau and the legal departments of the other Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will allow the proposed JSC to actively source for suitable judicial officers to serve in the various specialised Courts and to meet the challenges of the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: To ensure that we maintain a high level of trust in the judicial system, we need to ensure that our judicial officers are competent and able to dispense justice fairly, expeditiously and to answer the judicial needs for our future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am mindful that this proposal requires a Constitutional amendment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The key question is and has always been: how do we structure and design the Legal Service to continually build up our legal system and institutions?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This has never been and cannot be a one-off, static exercise; it is a continuous exercise of continuously tending to systematic institution building; to build and improve; to ensure that the structure we have works best for us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the years, we have systematically built up the Legal Service.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The enduring challenge has been our very small pool of talent, limited by our small size.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If we go back to the time of Independence, we had only 45 Legal Service Officers (LSOs) and a total of 130 members at the Bar.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: From those early days, we have always considered the Legal Service as a critical institution in establishing the rule of law in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is part of the DNA of Singapore's governance philosophy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Service provided a dedicated corps of officers who, amongst other things, built a strong, trusted Judiciary, prosecuted without fear or favour; supported effective, active and nimble policymaking; drafted all the laws that are passed by Parliament, and defended and secured Singapore’s interests internationally.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As Singapore grew and our legal system gained strength, it had to grow and modernise while maintaining high standards of excellence.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It had to attract its own share of talent and develop and deploy them well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As former Chief Justice and President of the LSC, the late Mr Yong Pung How, said, the Legal Service should be "positioned as a premier service in the public sector of Singapore".

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At that time and, for many years after, the small number of LSOs meant that a fully integrated model, where officers were actively deployed to both the Judicial and Legal Branches, better met our needs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Even in 2006, we only had 290 LSOs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: An integrated model was necessary for LSOs’ career progression and for the LSC to respond nimbly to personnel needs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It also had the benefit of providing a breadth of postings to develop young officers and ensuring future leaders had the necessary experience, spanning both the judicial and legal fields.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Existing Personnel Boards were restructured into two Boards, delineated along Branch lines.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Special Personnel Boards exercise jurisdiction over human resource functions, including promotions, of LSOs in respect of Grades below LSO Grade 2.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The integrated model, on the whole, was retained, particularly for those at the junior and senior ends of the spectrum.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This ensures that junior officers are developed in different fields of legal work, while preserving flexibility to deploy the limited number of senior officers to roles in both Branches and to meet the needs of the Service.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The proposal for a separate judicial service, separate from the Legal Service, has arisen over the years, including after 2014.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Looking at it, as the Legal Service is now, I would say there are pros and cons either way.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The challenge is to find the right balance for our circumstances and needs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A specialist model accounts for the widening spread of competencies which are needed in the Legal and Judicial Branches.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Officers have longer runways to acquire the skills and knowledge needed to operate in increasingly complex environments.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Each Service will have the ability to develop HR frameworks and talent development programmes, which can be targeted to their needs.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On the other hand, there are major benefits to an integrated model where officers rotate between Branches.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The opportunity for a varied career helps the Legal Service attract and retain talent.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For LSOs who assume senior leadership positions later on, rotations give them a better organisational perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: An integrated model also makes it easier to meet manpower needs, where more specialised capabilities are not required.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Each time this question has arisen, including as recently as last year, as Mr Murali Pillai pointed out, in November, we decided, in our view, the time was not quite right.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our relatively limited talent pool remains a challenge, albeit to a lesser degree.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But this is objectively a small number, operating in a small legal profession.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: England and Wales, for example, had almost 170,000 practising solicitors and barristers in 2020, making up around 0.28% of its population.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Singapore had fewer than 6,000 legal practitioners, constituting 0.1% of our population.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Yet, the UK still struggles to staff its judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2017, the House of Lords Select Committee on the Constitution expressed serious concern about recruitment to the bench.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The then-Lord Chancellor gave evidence that “not having enough people coming forward to be judges” was “one of the biggest threats” to the judiciary.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we left the door open for further consideration.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, the three Members have made very compelling points, which have been made previously, asking us to move further towards specialisation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They all identified the fast-paced disruptions to our legal environment and profession.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think we share common ground, in that the benefits of specialisation are likely to continue to grow in future, with smaller trade-offs as the Legal Service continues growing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the fundamental challenge of a limited talent pool remains.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Possibly, provided certain desirable features of our current system, like ensuring breadth of exposure, especially for younger officers, are retained in a sensible way.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The question then is, when is it the right time to move?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We could take a wait-and-see approach, maintain the current system, make small tweaks, in line with the changing environment.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We can also say, let us make the move now, to put ourselves on a better footing for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because, eventually, when the numbers grow further, it makes sense to split the two services anyway.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This matter has come up with the Members who spoke, as well as other Members who have spoken with us.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You have heard the points they have made, quite passionately.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That will also give us a better sense.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan had, in his speech, suggested this; we have moved ahead of the suggestion.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Working Group is co-chaired by the Attorney-General and Senior Judge Chao Hick Tin.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It comprises senior representatives from the Supreme Court, Attorney-General’s Chambers, Legal Service Commission Secretariat, MinLaw and Public Service Division.
